newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank seen leaving German rates on hold.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank seen leaving German rates on hold.

text.p: The Bundesbank, satisfied that the German economy is recovering without inflation, will leave interest rates unchanged at its council meeting on Thursday, analysts forecast.
All 10 economists surveyed by Reuters said the German central bank would keep rates on hold and only one predicted that there would be another cut in the discount and Lombard rates this year.
"We expect a clear improvement in the economy during the year," said Petra Koehler, economist at Dresdner Bank. "A cut in rates would not give any help."
All of the surveyed economists said they expected the Bundesbank to leave its key money market rate, the securities repurchase rate, fixed at three percent.
Earlier on Tuesday the Federal Statistics Office reported that consumer prices rose 1.5 percent year-on-year in March, down from a 1.7 percent pace in February.

Industrial output, which climbed 7.1 percent year-on-year in February, up from January's two percent annual growth rate, shows that the economy is picking up without additional monetary stimulation, economists said.
"The economy is recovering and there is still no inflation risk -- so there is no need for a rate reduction at the moment," said Alison Cottrell, economist at PaineWebber in London.
The Bundesbank last cut the discount and Lombard rates almost exactly a year ago to 2.50 and 4.50 percent, respectively.

Another key influence is the strength of the dollar, which has climbed to 37-month highs against the mark at near 1.73 marks. A strong dollar could lead to inflation in Germany as the mark price of imported goods, especially energy, climbs.
Economists said the Bundesbank had no reason to be alarmed just yet on this account but the currency market did limit the chances for a rate cut.

So far the strong dollar is only making it easier for German companies to export, giving the economy a lift and lessening the need for the central bank to prime the economic pump with lower interest rates, they said.
"We do not see a dollar in the future much stronger than today," said Alwin Schenk, economist at Sal. Oppenheim.

Although rates may be left steady, analysts will be keeping a close eye on the Bundesbank meeting because it will hold a news conference to announce its 1996 results, expected to show a smaller profit, and the size of its fund transfer to the federal government in Bonn.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel is hoping for a large infusion to help Germany reduce its budget deficit and qualify for European monetary union.
But economists expect a smaller profit in 1996 than 1995's 10.928 billion marks. Some 10.318 billion marks ($6 billion) of that profit was sent to Bonn.
They forecast a profit of between eight and 10 billion marks, with the decline mostly due to lower interest rates. The Bundesbank makes a profit by lending commercial banks money.
That would leave Bonn with little money left over to cut its deficit because seven billion marks of Bundesbank profit is already accounted for in the budget.
Analysts said several billion marks of Bundesbank profit would be a drop in the bucket anyway compared with the size of the public sector deficit -- expected to top 100 billion marks in 1997.

At the news conference, scheduled to start on Thursday at 1200 GMT, the central bank will provide further details of its accounts, including interest income from foreign and domestic credit institutions.
The Bundesbank's interest income in 1995 was 15.1 billion marks, while costs, mostly for personnel and other items such as the printing of money, were 4.7 billion.
--Frankfurt Newsroom + 49 69 756525 ($ = 1.730 German Marks)
